title: The thing that does not make sense in the model may be the clue that matters.
dek: Rory Sutherland's next introduction section argues that people often preserve meanings, rituals, and emotional protections that a stripped-down rational account cannot price correctly. The useful discipline is to notice when supposedly irrational behaviour is actually defending a human value the model erased.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: If a behaviour survives repeated pressure from logic, cost, or convenience, assume it may be protecting a human meaning before you assume people need to be corrected.

canon.heading: Sutherland: when logic strips away meaning, behaviour looks irrational only from the wrong distance.
canon.standfirst: Read the introduction section "Some Things Are Dishwasher-Proof, Others Are Reason-Proof" from Rory Sutherland's Alchemy, through PDF page 25. Sutherland argues that many choices resist neat rational explanation because they carry emotional, symbolic, and contextual value that standard optimisation models are bad at noticing.
canon.readerIntro: Read this section for the pattern beneath the anecdotes. Sutherland is not saying reason is useless; he is showing that reason often measures only the visible utility while missing the social or psychological function that makes a choice worth keeping. Mark each example where an apparently wasteful preference turns out to protect dignity, ritual, reassurance, or felt significance.

blocks.label: 01 / Rational simplification can destroy the value it is trying to explain
paragraphs: Sutherland's point is not merely that people are inconsistent. It is that many forms of value stop looking sensible once a model reduces them to speed, cost, or functional utility alone. In that reduction, the explanation becomes cleaner while the human truth becomes thinner.

That is why this section matters for commercial judgement. When a team asks only what is cheapest, fastest, or most efficient, it may remove the very ingredient that made the experience reassuring, flattering, ceremonial, or worth talking about.

blocks.label: 02 / Seemingly irrational preferences often protect status, trust, or emotional safety
paragraphs: The examples work because they force a distinction between literal function and perceived meaning. A behaviour can survive a logical attack if it performs a social or emotional job that the attack refuses to count. To the spreadsheet, the preference looks silly; to the person living inside the choice, it may feel prudent or humane.

This is a useful correction for research and strategy. If customers persist with a habit that appears inefficient, the first question is not how to educate them out of it. The first question is what hidden loss they think the efficient option would impose.

blocks.label: 03 / Better persuasion starts by finding the missing variable
paragraphs: Sutherland's broader argument is that good persuasion often comes from changing the meaning of a choice rather than only improving its literal economics. Once you understand the unpriced variable, you can redesign the offer, the framing, or the ritual around it.

That makes this reading practical. Instead of arguing harder for the sensible option, look for the invisible cost the audience believes they are paying: embarrassment, uncertainty, disrespect, diminished pleasure, or loss of control.

blocks.label: 04 / The challenge is not to abandon reason but to widen what reason is allowed to see
paragraphs: Sutherland is not proposing mysticism as a substitute for judgement. He is pushing against a narrow definition of evidence that discounts everything people cannot justify with tidy language. The corrective is to admit that observed behaviour may reveal motives the respondent cannot articulate cleanly.

Use the section as a guardrail against sterile optimisation. A better model of choice does not ignore efficiency; it places efficiency among other human goods that may matter more at the point of decision.

not everything that matters is measurable
closeReading: What kind of value does Sutherland think standard rational explanation most often erase: social meaning, emotional reassurance, ritual, status, or something else?
Choose one preference from your work that currently looks inefficient. What hidden loss might the user believe the efficient option would create?
Where in this section does Sutherland shift from mocking narrow logic to offering a more useful account of behaviour?
Take one product decision your team treats as obvious. Which missing variable could make the rejected option feel safer, kinder, more prestigious, or more trustworthy to the buyer?
How would you redesign one offer if you had to preserve the emotional function of the old behaviour while still improving convenience or cost?

principle.heading: When behaviour resists logic, inspect the missing meaning before you optimize it away.
principle.body: A clean argument about efficiency is weak if it ignores the human job a habit performs. Before removing friction, cost, or ornament, ask what dignity, confidence, pleasure, or signal the current behaviour is protecting.
principle.example: A bank wants more customers to switch from in-branch service to a cheaper digital flow. The rational case is obvious: the app is faster and always available. Adoption stalls because the branch visit is not merely a transaction for some customers; it is reassurance that a serious person can confirm the decision, answer questions, and witness the transfer. A stronger design keeps the digital flow but adds visible human confirmation at the moment of uncertainty.
principle.practice: Choose one 'irrational' customer behaviour from a live product or offer. Write the efficient alternative your team prefers, then list three human functions the current behaviour might be serving. Redesign the preferred option so it preserves at least one of those functions instead of merely arguing against it.

signals.heading: Three signals about how platforms are turning capability into a fuller product story instead of a single feature claim.

fieldNotes.title: Google used the Pixel event to widen the meaning of the device, not just refresh the hardware
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reported that Google introduced the Pixel 11 line, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Tag, and a larger set of Gemini-powered features at Made by Google 2026, including sign-language support, more natural voice input, and tighter camera-to-search behavior.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: This fits Sutherland's point that buyers do not evaluate a product only as raw specification. Google is trying to make the phone feel like a more fluent assistant and accessibility tool, which is a broader emotional and practical promise than a camera bump or chip upgrade alone.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether buyers respond more strongly to the integrated experience story than to the higher prices and modest hardware changes across the lineup.

fieldNotes.title: Gemini's growth suggests AI habit is now being measured at platform scale
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reported that Google's Gemini app has surged to 1 billion users, giving Google a public adoption marker that moves the story from model capability toward repeated consumer use.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A billion-user signal changes the strategic question. Once an AI tool becomes ordinary enough to sit inside everyday routines, the advantage shifts from novelty to trust, speed, and how cleanly the tool fits the moments when people actually reach for help.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether Google can turn broad Gemini reach into deeper repeated behavior across search, Android, and commerce rather than a large but shallow user base.

fieldNotes.title: Google is packaging reassurance into tracking, not just location data
fieldNotes.whatHappened: TechCrunch reported that Google launched the $29 Pixel Tag, a new tracker for keys, wallets, and luggage that plugs into Android's Find Hub network and can also be located from a Pixel Watch or by asking Gemini.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Trackers sell on relief more than on technical architecture. The meaningful product promise is not merely that another tag exists, but that the user can offload a small recurring anxiety into a network, a watch, and a voice assistant that feel close at hand.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether Google's tighter connection between Find Hub, wearables, and Gemini makes the tag feel like part of a dependable system rather than a copycat accessory.

tweets.author: zam
tweets.title: A startup wins when the new physics force a new story
tweets.summary: This is worth keeping because it treats narrative as part of the operating system, not decoration. A strange technical or market bet has to become desirable before incumbents copy it, and the company has to keep moving fast enough that the story remains attached to real progress.
tweets.text:
POV: you’re 34 years old and your brief career as a self-made solo AI entrepreneur / CEO / B2B SaaS founder is finally over.

You’re back in corporate, working a mid-level job at a fintech whose app occasionally duplicates transactions and shows negative balances.

The market changed. Two years ago recruiters begged you to “just have a conversation.” Now you’ve exhausted your entire network to land $180k TC.

And… it’s actually kind of nice.

There are snacks in the office. Free coffee. The sparkling water fridge is always full. You order a better Uber without guilt because you have a salary again.

You move Jira tickets around a little. Claude got smarter and can vibe-code half your tasks before your manager realizes it.

Suddenly you have free time. More importantly, you have money.

Your wife stops asking when the startup is going to make revenue. You send her to Barry’s with her friends while you stay late at the office “working.”

Before flying home from your first vacation in two years, she gets brunch with the girls in Palo Alto.

Maybe the real exit was getting a W-2.

output.heading: Complete one reason-proof audit.
output.body: Keep one live behaviour on the page that your team currently calls irrational. Your output is a short audit of the hidden meaning it may be protecting and one redesign that preserves that meaning while improving the experience.
